```yaml title="release-check.yaml"
              card: {kind: Artifact, name: company-sharing-policy, version: 0.1.0}
              path: extracted/company-sharing-policy.pdf.json
    - id: destination-restricted
      statement: The destination restricts access to the report.
      check: {kind: assert, path: inputs.destination.restricted, operator: equals, expected: true}

```

Two are assertions. `recipient-authorized` compares `inputs.recipient.authorized` with `true`, and `destination-restricted` compares `inputs.destination.restricted` with `true`. Both read facts the application supplies in the request. Wyrd does not query an authorization service here: it judges what the application reports that lookup returned, so the origin of that fact is the application's to record. Like the log line in [Foundations](/wyrd/understand/foundations-of-verification/#what-is-being-checked-and-against-what), the check is no better than that supplied fact; the example keeps it simple, and a production Verifier can instead receive the lookup's own response, or check the lookup call in a trace. `follows-policy` is a model judge. An Agent reads the purpose, the report, the recipient, and the extracted policy, then decides whether the policy permits the release.

The [Quickstart](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/) declares the same Verifier in Python, Rust, or TypeScript and runs it.

## How a Verifier declares requirements

A Verifier has four parts:

| Part | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `inputs` | Named evidence slots the caller fills, each with a `type` and an optional schema |
| `steps` | Optional preparation, such as extracting text from a file |
| `requirements` | Each has an `id`, a `statement`, and one `check`, and gets its own outcome |
| `decide` | How requirement outcomes combine: `all`, the default, or a `pass_rate`. `release-check` omits it, so `all` applies |

Because a binding supplies the subject, one Verifier can check many Cards. [Verifier Card](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/) lists every field, input type, step, and check.

When `metadata.version` is omitted, the server assigns `0.1.0`, then the next patch version each time the content changes.

_Diagram `verification-parts`: see the web page._

### Steps and checks

A step prepares evidence, such as the text of a PDF, and its output feeds later steps and checks. A check decides one requirement. Each has a `kind`, and some kinds only make sense in one role:

| Kind | Used as | Produces or decides | Use it when | Runs in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `assert` | check | Compares one value from an input or step output with an operator | The rule is a field comparison: a status equals `approved`, a reply does not contain "guaranteed" | Check engine |
| `trace` | check | Compares values selected from the spans of a trace | The rule is about what your code did, such as calling the order lookup before replying | Check engine |
| `drift` | check | Compares a window of samples with a baseline | You care whether inputs or outputs shift over time, not whether one answer is right | Check engine, on a schedule |
| `extract` | step | The text and structure of a file | A later check or Agent needs to read a PDF, DOCX, XLSX, or other document | Check engine |
| `code` | step or check | As a step, JSON; as a check, a verdict | The rule is deterministic, but no operator expresses it | Monty pool |
| `agent` | step or check | As a step, the Agent's response; as a check, a verdict | The rule needs judgment: meaning, tone, or policy | LLM gateway |

The cheapest kind that catches the failure is the usual starting point. The check engine needs no model and no Python; an `agent` check costs a model call each time it runs.

The Monty pool is sandboxed Python: a fresh worker per call that the server starts from its own binary. An `agent` step or check runs an Agent whose model calls go through the LLM gateway. Step and check Agents follow the same rules: each can call the [built-in tools](/wyrd/reference/agent-tools-and-authorization/) it declares, and every call still needs its own grants. [Recipes](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/verifier-recipes/) has a working Verifier for each kind.

### Workspaces and fixed policy files

An Agent that reads files works in a workspace. The Verifier maps paths under `/inputs` to evidence: an input slot such as `inputs.policy`, or files of an uploaded Artifact Card. `release-check` mounts the extracted text of `company-sharing-policy@0.1.0`. The Agent explores its files with `fs.list`, `fs.read`, and `fs.search`, and can run `code.run` over them.

An Artifact selection is part of the Verifier version. Uploading a newer version of that Artifact does not change what the Verifier reads, and a caller cannot replace the files at run time. To judge against a new policy, declare the Verifier again with the new file, which registers a new Verifier version; the Quickstart's [policy update](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/#5-update-the-policy) creates `release-check@0.1.1`. A selection that matches no file fails before any model call.

Files are mounted unchanged and unparsed. `fs.read` and `fs.search` serve raw text, so they refuse or skip a PDF until the Agent calls `fs.extract`, which writes its extraction JSON under `/work`. `/work` is scratch for one call and is never evidence: a citation names the `/inputs` file's `attachment_<n>` slot, not a `/work` path. [Uploaded files](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/verifier-recipes/#uploaded-files) shows the upload and the mount.

### Bindings

A binding attaches a Verifier to what it checks, under `verified_by`. It can sit on a Service, on one of its components (an Agent, Model, Data, Prompt, or any other Card the Service uses), or on a standalone Agent. A binding can also name a Trigger in `runs_on`, so the server runs it on a schedule, and Operators in `on_failure`. On a [Repository](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/declare-a-repository/), the `pull_request` Trigger queues one execution per binding for each new head or base of a ready pull request. Each execution is pinned to that source and to the policy selected when GitHub's delivery was accepted, and a newer source cancels the older one's unfinished work.

## Code or YAML

A Verifier, and every other Card, can be declared in two ways. Both produce the same Cards, and the server can't tell them apart.

- **In code.** The Python, Rust, and TypeScript SDKs build Cards with the same field names as the YAML. This is the quickest way to start: one program declares the Cards and verifies with them. The [Quickstart](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/) and [Author in code](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/author-in-code/) use this route.
- **In YAML files.** Each Card is a file that lives in the repository beside the application. This is the recommended route in production. Any language can declare the same files, a change to a requirement is reviewed in a pull request like any other change, and CI declares the files with `wyrd declare` before the application deploys. The [Build and verify](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/define-a-service/) guides and [Deploy a Service from CI](/wyrd/operate/deploy-a-service-from-ci/) use this route.

A team can start in code and move to YAML later, because both routes declare the same Cards.

## Calls, verdicts, and failures

### verify and submit

Wyrd runs a Verifier on three paths. They differ in when the verdict arrives, and so in which decision it can inform:

| Path | Called with | Verdict arrives | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Inline | `verify` | In the call's response | The application must decide before it responds or acts |
| Queued | `submit` | Later; any process holding the execution can wait for it | The decision can wait, a model judge is too slow for the request, or evidence such as trace spans lands after the call |
| Scheduled | A binding with a Trigger in `runs_on` | When the server runs the schedule | A time window of recorded samples needs judging. Only drift Verifiers are scheduled, and they refuse `verify` |

`verify` runs the Verifier now and returns the result. These calls use `no-refund-promise`, the Verifier from the [setup check](/wyrd/get-started/setup/#3-check-it-end-to-end). A `failed` verdict is an ordinary value, not an exception:

```python
result = run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", answer="Your refund request is approved.")
```

`submit` returns once its inputs are staged, and the server then queues an execution that any process holding it can wait on:

```python
execution = run.observe.submit("no-refund-promise", answer="You have a guaranteed refund.")
result = execution.wait(60)
```

_Diagram `verification-paths`: see the web page._

Drift Verifiers judge samples over a time window, so they refuse `verify`. Their `submit` records samples, and a scheduled binding judges the window. Wyrd schedules only drift. To run any other Verifier on a recurring basis, call `submit` from the application's own scheduler.

### Verdicts

With `all`, any failed requirement fails the Verifier. Otherwise any inconclusive requirement makes it inconclusive. Otherwise it passes. A requirement is `not_applicable` when the step it belongs to is skipped because its `when` condition does not hold; those requirements do not count, and a Verifier with no applicable requirement is inconclusive.

`inconclusive` means no judgment was possible, such as missing evidence or an error inside one check. An error or timeout of the whole call or execution is different: it produces no verdict at all. `inconclusive` is never a pass, and never a claim that the subject failed.

An `agent` or `code` check can also return a `data` object beside its verdict, such as a score or labels, when its `response_format` declares a schema for it. The server checks the whole response against that schema. A response that does not match makes the requirement `inconclusive` and keeps no data, so a requirement's `data` is either valid or absent. [Custom data](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/#custom-data) has the schema rules and size limits.

_Diagram `run-lifecycle`: see the web page._

A queued execution has a status before it has a verdict: `pending`, `running`, `retrying`, `completed`, `cancelled`, `timed_out`, or `errored`. `completed` means it produced a result; `timed_out` and `errored` mean no check finished, so there is no verdict and no Operator runs.

### Missing evidence, timeouts, and errors

Each outcome that is not a pass has a defined meaning, and the application decides its response to each:

| Situation | `verify` returns | Queued execution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An input slot is omitted | The requirements that need it are `inconclusive` | The same |
| A trace has no visible spans yet | The `trace` check is `inconclusive` at once | Tries 3 times, then `inconclusive` |
| A model judge cannot decide, or passes without a valid citation | That requirement is `inconclusive` | The same |
| The call exceeds the timeout | `WYRD_VERIFICATION_504_EXECUTION_TIMED_OUT`, no verdict | Status `timed_out`, no verdict |
| The input does not match the Verifier | `WYRD_VERIFICATION_400_INPUT_INVALID`; nothing ran | No verdict: `submit` is refused or the execution ends `errored` |

An error or a timeout is no verdict at all. The finance API releases only `passed` reports, so every other outcome holds the report. [Error codes](/wyrd/api/errors/) lists every code.

### Trace evidence

A `trace` check judges the whole trace. It reads every retained span with that trace ID from `bifrost.traces.spans`, whatever Service, Card, or time each span carries, ordered by start time and then span ID. The read is an ordinary query by the account the execution runs as, so the same permissions, tenant boundary, and audit apply. Each attempt reads a trace once, and every check in the Verifier that names that trace judges the same spans.

The check is `inconclusive`, never judged on part of a trace, when the trace has more than 10,000 spans, the query is refused or fails, the read times out, a span cannot be decoded, or the input supplied no trace. A selector that matches no span compares `null`.

Spans can land after the call that verifies them. A trace with no visible span has not landed yet, and the outcome depends on the path:

- `verify` judges the check `inconclusive` at once.
- A queued execution, from `submit` or a schedule, stops the attempt with error code `evidence_unavailable` and status `retrying`, and records no result. It tries 3 times, waiting 30 seconds and then 60 seconds. The last attempt judges the check `inconclusive` and completes under the Verifier's `decide` rule.

A completed result is final. Spans that land after it are judged only by a new execution.

### Operators

An Operator reacts when a scheduled execution of a binding returns `failed`, by sending a Slack or PagerDuty notification or calling a URL. `verify` and `submit` never run Operators; your code reads their verdicts.

## Where the time goes

Whether a verdict fits a request depends on the application's deadline and on which checks the Verifier runs. Time in a `verify` call falls into three parts.

**Engine and coordination.** The server resolves the exact Verifier and subject, checks the caller's `verifier:run` permission, and admits the work. Resolved targets are cached in each server process, per tenant, Verifier, and subject. A first call, an evicted entry, or a change to the Verifier reads PostgreSQL to reload; while the process cannot hear change notifications, every call reads PostgreSQL. Admission can refuse work instead of queueing it: `WYRD_VERIFICATION_429_STAGING_FULL` when staging is full, `WYRD_SERVER_503_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` when no Python worker or workspace is free.

**Evidence.** JSON evidence arrives in the request. A `File` is hashed by the SDK, which uploads only digests the server lacks, so a repeated file uploads once; each execution resolves its file and Artifact metadata once and reuses it. A step such as PDF extraction, or a `trace` check that reads spans from Bifrost, adds its own read time.

**Checks.** An `assert` or `trace` check runs in the check engine without a model. A `code` check runs in a sandboxed Python worker. An `agent` check calls a model through the LLM gateway, possibly several times with tool calls between them, and usually dominates the total. In the finance example, the two assertions add little; the policy judge (`policy-judge.yaml` in the Quickstart) adds up to three model calls (`max_iterations: 3`), shared between tool use and answer corrections.

The whole call is bounded by `WYRD_VERIFICATION_TIMEOUT_MS`, 60 seconds by default ([Runtime limits](/wyrd/reference/verification-runtime-limits/)). That is a bound, not a latency guarantee, and Wyrd publishes no general latency figure. Only a measurement of the deployed Verifier, on its real evidence and model routes, shows whether it fits.

## What Wyrd retains, and how requirements change

Wyrd returns the verdict, then writes its record in the background, so storage does not slow the request. Once committed to Bifrost's write-ahead log, the record is durable; a server stop or write failure before that can lose it. Either way, the verdict the application received stands.

Stored results live in three Bifrost tables, all queryable with SQL: each result's summary in `bifrost.verification.results`, its requirement outcomes and steps in `bifrost.verification.execution_outputs`, and its inputs in `bifrost.verification.execution_inputs`. The result the call returns is compact: the verdict and each requirement's outcome. The checks, provenance, step outputs, and pinned evidence stay in storage for later inspection, as the Quickstart's [stored verdicts](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/#4-confirm-the-stored-verdicts) step shows. [Runs and evidence](/wyrd/understand/runs-observations-and-evidence/) and [Bifrost](/wyrd/understand/bifrost/) explain retention and query visibility.

Every stored result names the exact Verifier and subject versions it judged, including the policy file the Verifier version mounted. Declaring a new Verifier version for a changed policy does not retarget old results: those judged by `release-check@0.1.0` still name the original policy, so a past decision can be traced to the policy it applied. [Cards and versions](/wyrd/understand/cards-versions-and-relationships/) explains versioning.

## Next

The [Quickstart](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/) runs the finance example, and [Verify during a request](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/verify-a-request-in-real-time/), [Verify an agent's workflow](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/verify-an-agent-workflow/), [Check on a schedule](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/monitor-drift/), and [Investigate a failed verification](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/run-a-verification-and-inspect-its-evidence/) run each path on this page. [Write verifiable requirements](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/write-verifiable-requirements/), [Establish sufficient evidence](/wyrd/build-and-verify/observe/establish-sufficient-evidence/), and [Act on verdicts in production](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/act-on-verdicts-in-production/) apply this to your own system, and the [Verifier Card reference](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/) lists every field.

# Runs and evidence

Page: /wyrd/understand/runs-observations-and-evidence/

> How Wyrd records what a declared service actually does, and ties each observation to the version that ran.

An observation is a record of what a declared service actually did. Each one is tied to the exact Card version and the run that produced it.

## A run is one invocation

A run is one execution of a service, such as answering one question. Every observation recorded inside it shares the same `run_id`:

**Python**

```python
with state.run("agent") as run:
    answer = answer_question(question)
    run.bifrost.write({"question": question, "answer": answer})
```

**Rust**

```rust
let run = state.run_for_card("agent")?;
let answer = answer_question(question).await?;
run.bifrost()
    .write(&json!({ "question": question, "answer": answer }))
    .await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const run = state.run("agent");
const answer = await answerQuestion(question);
await run.bifrost.write({ question, answer });
```

`state` holds the exact Card versions the service runs. `state.run("agent")` scopes the run to the Card behind the `agent` alias, and `run.for_card(alias)` scopes the same run to another one. Opening a run makes no network call.

## Where observations land

Observations go to Bifrost, the Wyrd data plane:

| Recorded with | Lands in |
| --- | --- |
| `bifrost.write(row)` | The active `bifrost.datasets.<name>` table |
| `bifrost.write_to(table, row)` | The named `bifrost.datasets.<name>` table |
| `observe.verify` and `observe.submit` | `bifrost.verification.execution_inputs` and `bifrost.verification.results` |
| Drift samples, with `observe.submit` | `bifrost.drift.observations` |
| OpenTelemetry spans, metrics, and logs | `bifrost.traces.spans`, `bifrost.metrics.points`, and `bifrost.logs.records` |

The active table is the Service's table when it declares exactly one. A Service with several has none until the program binds one with `state.use_table_by_name(table)`, and every run of that state then shares it, so runs writing different tables at once name each with `write_to` (`writeTo` in TypeScript).

Every row carries its `subject_card_uid`, its `run_id`, and the principal that wrote it. A service may write only about Cards in its own graph. Anything else fails with `WYRD_VALA_403_BIFROST_CARD_SCOPE` ([Errors](/wyrd/api/errors/)).

## Recording is buffered

`bifrost.write` and the sample path of `observe.submit` queue the row; a returned call means the row is queued, not stored. `shutdown` sends everything still queued, so a process that exits without it loses those rows. If the queue fills, the call fails with `WYRD_CLIENT_429_QUEUE_FULL` instead of blocking.

A row the server has stored can take a moment to show up in queries. [Bifrost](/wyrd/understand/bifrost/) explains why.

## Evidence joins on the run

Observations and verdicts share `run_id`, so one SQL query joins what a run saw to how it was judged:

```sql
SELECT t.question, t.answer, r.verdict, r.verifier_version
FROM bifrost.datasets.tickets AS t
JOIN bifrost.verification.results AS r ON r.run_id = t.run_id
```

## Next

[Bifrost](/wyrd/understand/bifrost/).

# Cards and versions

Page: /wyrd/understand/cards-versions-and-relationships/

> A Service declaration is a set of versioned Cards, each one a declared component of an AI system.

A Card is a versioned declaration of one AI system component, or of one Verifier that checks components. Every observation and verdict points back to an exact Card version.

## The shape of a Card

This is the Service Card from the [setup check](/wyrd/get-started/setup/#3-check-it-end-to-end):

```yaml title="support-reply.yaml"
# The subject: your support app's Service, verified by no-refund-promise.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: support-reply
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  verified_by:
    - verifier: ./no-refund-promise.yaml

```

An author writes `apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata`, and `spec`. The server adds `relationships` and `status`.

A Card is identified by `space`, `kind`, `name`, and `version`. A space groups related Cards. An omitted space comes from `wyrd.toml`, or is `default`.

## Versions are exact

A reference names either a file, relative to the file it is in, or a declared Card at an exact version:

```yaml
verifier: ./no-refund-promise.yaml
verifier: {kind: Verifier, name: no-refund-promise, version: 1.0.0}
```

In [code](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/author-in-code/), a definition passed where a reference goes takes the place of the file.

So a declared Service records exactly which Cards it was built from, and a verdict points back to exactly what ran. A Card moves to a new version of a dependency only when its reference changes and it is declared again.

`metadata.version` is optional. Without it, Wyrd records `0.1.0`, then the next patch version each time the content changes. Declaring unchanged content keeps the current version. Re-declaring an exact version with different content fails with `WYRD_REGISTRY_409_SPEC_DRIFT`.

## Relationships come from references

The server reads every reference in a Card's `spec` and records it in both directions:

```text
Service support-reply
└── Verifier no-refund-promise
```

Every Card therefore shows what it depends on and what depends on it. A running service may record observations only about Cards in its own graph.

## Next

[How verification works in Wyrd](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/).

# Bifrost

Page: /wyrd/understand/bifrost/

> Wyrd's analytical warehouse, the two ways to write to it, and when a written row becomes queryable.

Bifrost is the analytical warehouse inside every Wyrd server. Observations, verdicts, traces, audit records, and caller-owned rows all land in it as tables that read-only SQL can query:

```sql
SELECT verdict, count(*) AS executions
FROM bifrost.verification.results
GROUP BY verdict
```

## How it is put together

_Diagram `bifrost-parts`: see the web page._

| Part | Does |
| --- | --- |
| Gate | Checks each request's permission and routes it |
| Scribe | Accepts writes and publishes them into tables |
| Oracle | Runs SQL queries |
| Forge | Compacts files and applies retention in the background |

One server runs all four.

Tables are Apache Iceberg tables of Parquet files in the deployment's object store, with the catalog in Postgres. The `bifrost.datasets` namespace holds caller-owned tables. Wyrd writes every other namespace.

## Where each part runs

Every pod runs the same `wyrd-server` binary, and `WYRD_TARGET` picks which parts it runs. The default, `combined`, runs every part, so a single pod is a complete deployment. A larger team splits writes, queries, and compaction so each scales on its own load.

_Diagram `bifrost-pods`: see the web page._

## Two ways in

Inside a running service, `run.observe.*` writes rows tied to the run and the exact Card version. For batch jobs, backfills, and notebooks, the `Bifrost` client registers tables, writes rows, and queries them. SQL is read-only.

## Written versus queryable

_Diagram `bifrost-write-read`: see the web page._

A row is stored once a Scribe acknowledges it, which is what `flush` and `shutdown` wait for. It becomes queryable when it is published, shortly after. Queries also read the recent unpublished rows each Scribe still holds, and a row published while the query runs is returned exactly once.

Every query ends with a status: `success`; `degraded` when a Scribe could not be reached as the query listed its sources, so that Scribe's recent rows may be missing; or `failed`, which includes losing a Scribe after the query has read its recent rows. The SDKs raise an error on `failed`. Query errors are listed in [Errors](/wyrd/api/errors/).

## Next

[Identity and authorization](/wyrd/understand/identity-and-authorization/).

# Identity and access

Page: /wyrd/understand/identity-and-authorization/

> Every call to Wyrd is made as an account whose roles decide what it may do; a running Service also names its exact release, from its bundle.

Every call to the Wyrd server is made as an account, and the account's roles decide what it may do. A running Service adds one fact the key cannot carry: which exact release it is, which comes from its bundle.

## Tenants

Every account belongs to exactly one tenant. A tenant is a hard isolation boundary: PostgreSQL row-level security keeps every query inside its tenant. Platform administrators create and suspend tenants but are never implicitly authorized over a tenant's resources.

## Accounts

| Account | Used by | Created |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User | A person | On first sign-in through the tenant's identity provider |
| Tenant administrator | The first administrator | When the tenant is set up |
| Service account | CI, a running Service, any automation | By an administrator, with `wyrd principal credential create-principal` |

Declaring a Card creates no account. One Service account serves every release of its Service, so a new release needs no new account and no new key. [Deploy a Service from CI](/wyrd/operate/deploy-a-service-from-ci/) sets up the usual pair: one account for CI, one per running Service.

## The key and the release

A Service account's key says who is calling. The release is the exact Service Card version, which the server knows by its UID.

A running application gets the UID from its bundle. `WyrdState` sends it with the key on every call, and the server limits that call to the release's own Cards: an observation about a Model the release does not use is refused. Each row then records both, the account in `sub_principal_id` and `act_principal_id`, the release in `workload_card_uid`, and the Card observed in `subject_card_uid`.

Two releases can run at once with the same key. Each bundle names its own UID, so their evidence never mixes.

A User, or a Service account created without `--workload-name`, needs no release. It can record and verify evidence for any registered Card its roles allow; that evidence has no release.

## One account per Service

`--workload-name checkout` restricts an account to releases of the `checkout` Service. A restricted account must name a release to record or verify Card evidence, and only a `checkout` release.

Each Service has at most one restricted account, and its scheduled Verifiers run as that account. A schedule runs only while that account has used the release in the last 24 hours, so a retired release stops being checked on its own. A Service with no restricted account has no scheduled verification.

## Keys and tokens

The client exchanges a key for an access token that lasts 5 minutes, and renews it automatically. A role change reaches a running Service at its next renewal. An account can hold several keys, which is how keys rotate: issue a new key, deploy it, then revoke the old one.

## Roles

A permission is written `resource:action`, such as `cards:write`. A role is a set of permissions. Every tenant has four built-in roles, each including everything in the one above it:

| Role | Adds | Typical holder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `viewer` | Reading Cards, results, the audit log, and Bifrost tables | A person who inspects results |
| `workload` | Recording Runs and observations, running Verifiers, calling the LLM gateway | A running Service |
| `editor` | Declaring and deleting Cards, uploading artifacts | CI, or a person who changes declarations |
| `admin` | Everything, including accounts, keys, and gateway settings | The tenant administrator |

Roles apply to the whole tenant. `workload` cannot change a Card, so a running Service cannot change what it is verified against.

## Every decision is audited

Wyrd checks the permission before the operation proceeds. Each `allowed` or `denied` decision is recorded in the background in `bifrost.system.audit_log`, a Bifrost table a `viewer` can query.

# Architecture

Page: /wyrd/understand/architecture/

> What a team deployment of Wyrd runs, what it connects to, and why each part is separate.

A Wyrd deployment is one server binary, run as one pod or as several pods with different roles, behind one endpoint you own. It stores everything durable in Postgres and object storage, so pods can be replaced, scaled, or split by role without moving data.

_Diagram `wyrd-deployment`: see the web page._

## One binary, several roles

Every pod runs `wyrd-server`. `WYRD_TARGET` chooses what a pod does: `combined` runs everything and is a complete deployment on its own. `direct` runs synchronous verification, `worker` runs queued verification and GitHub webhooks, and `bifrost-ingest`, `bifrost-query`, and `bifrost-maintenance` run writes, queries, and compaction, so each scales on its own load. A pod refuses verification work its target does not run with `WYRD_VERIFICATION_421_WRONG_TARGET`. Splitting changes resource ownership, not the API: clients see one server either way. [Bifrost](/wyrd/understand/bifrost/#where-each-part-runs) shows which part each target runs.

## One endpoint

Your load balancer owns the public address and TLS. It routes requests but never establishes who the caller is; every request carries a Wyrd token, and the server checks its roles and tenant. Pods talk to each other over mutual TLS.

## Postgres and object storage

Postgres holds declarations and their versions, principals and roles, and the coordination state that lets many pods share work. Object storage holds evidence, artifacts, and Bifrost's Parquet tables. Neither lives on a pod, which is why a pod can be lost without losing a verdict.

## Identity

People sign in through your OIDC identity provider. Apps, CI, and agents use Service account keys. [Identity and authorization](/wyrd/understand/identity-and-authorization/) explains principals, roles, and tenants.

## Model calls

The server calls model providers with keys you configure, for model-judged checks and for apps that route their calls through the LLM gateway. Wyrd never hosts a model.

## Next

[How verification works in Wyrd](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/) follows one check through the server. [Bifrost](/wyrd/understand/bifrost/) covers the data plane.

# Technical questions

Page: /wyrd/understand/technical-questions/

> Direct answers on real-time verification: who enforces a verdict, missing evidence, timeouts, model providers, sensitive data, versions, and self-hosting.

These are direct answers to the questions engineers ask before adopting Wyrd. Each links to the page that owns the detail.

## Does Wyrd block a response that fails?

No. Wyrd returns a verdict; your application decides what to do with it. In the [finance API](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/#one-verification-end-to-end), the handler releases a report only when `result.passed` is true and holds it otherwise. If the handler ignored the verdict, nothing would stop the release.

Enforcement lives in your code because the right response depends on the action: hold a report, rewrite a reply, ask a person, or log and continue. Executions a binding's Trigger creates can also notify through an [Operator](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/#operators), which reports a failure but does not undo anything.

## When should I use verify, submit, or a schedule?

Use `verify` when the application must decide before it responds or acts. Use `submit` when the decision can wait, the check is too slow for the request, or the evidence lands after the call. Use a schedule to judge a time window of recorded samples, as with drift. [verify and submit](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/#verify-and-submit) compares the three; [Verify during a request](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/verify-a-request-in-real-time/) and [Check on a schedule](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/monitor-drift/) run the first and the last. `verify` and `submit` run the same Verifier; schedules judge drift Verifiers, which refuse `verify`.

## What happens when evidence is missing?

The requirements that need the missing evidence come back `inconclusive`, and the others are judged normally. With the default decision rule, any inconclusive requirement makes the verdict inconclusive unless another requirement failed. `inconclusive` is never a pass and never a claim that the subject failed.

A trace that has not landed yet is a special case: `verify` judges the `trace` check inconclusive at once, and a queued execution tries 3 times before it does. A missing trace on its own does not prove an action was skipped. [Trace evidence](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/#trace-evidence) has the rules.

## What happens on a timeout or an error?

A `verify` call that runs past `WYRD_VERIFICATION_TIMEOUT_MS` (60 seconds by default) returns `WYRD_VERIFICATION_504_EXECUTION_TIMED_OUT` and no verdict. The SDK does not retry it, so your code chooses the fallback. Invalid input is refused with a typed error before anything runs. A queued execution that times out or errors has status `timed_out` or `errored` and no verdict.

Treat every outcome except `passed` as not passed. [Runtime limits](/wyrd/reference/verification-runtime-limits/#if-a-limit-is-reached) lists each limit and its result, and [Error codes](/wyrd/api/errors/) lists every code.

## How fast is a real-time check?

It depends on the checks. Assertions and trace checks run without a model; a model judge adds at least one model call and usually dominates. Wyrd publishes no general latency figure, because the total depends on your Verifier, evidence, model, and provider. Measure the Verifier you deploy. [Where the time goes](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/#where-the-time-goes) separates engine, evidence, and check time.

## What does a model provider see?

An `agent` check sends its prompt, with the evidence the prompt includes, to the model provider through your server's [LLM gateway](/wyrd/connect/set-up-the-llm-gateway/). Anything the Agent reads with a tool, such as a policy file through `fs.read`, is sent too. The provider key stays on the server, and each tool call needs its own [grants](/wyrd/reference/agent-tools-and-authorization/).

Assertion, trace, and code checks send nothing to a provider. Keep sensitive evidence out of model checks when a deterministic check can decide the requirement, and use synthetic data while you build.

## Can I trust a model judge?

Not without testing it. A model judge can be biased, inconsistent, or wrong, and agreement with another model is not independent evidence. Wyrd requires a judge that passes to cite the evidence it used, and makes the requirement `inconclusive` when it does not; it does not measure a judge's accuracy for you. Run the judge on labeled cases before relying on it, as in [Choose checks and test judges](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/write-verifiable-requirements/#3-choose-checks-and-test-judges). [Can an AI judge be trusted?](/wyrd/understand/foundations-of-verification/#can-an-ai-judge-be-trusted) summarizes what research shows.

## What happens to old results when a requirement changes?

They keep their versions. Every result names the exact Verifier and subject versions it judged, and a changed Verifier, or a changed file it mounts, becomes a new version. The [Quickstart](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/#5-update-the-policy) shows a policy update creating `release-check@0.1.1` while results from `0.1.0` still name the original policy. [Cards and versions](/wyrd/understand/cards-versions-and-relationships/) explains versioning.

## Where is the evidence kept?

Each result's summary goes to `bifrost.verification.results`, its requirement outcomes and steps to `bifrost.verification.execution_outputs`, and the pinned inputs to `bifrost.verification.execution_inputs`, all queryable with SQL. The server writes them in the background after it answers. A record is durable once committed to Bifrost's write-ahead log; a server stop or write failure before that can lose it. [What Wyrd retains](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/#what-wyrd-retains-and-how-requirements-change) explains the boundary.

## Which languages are supported?

Python, Rust, and TypeScript have first-class SDKs with the same calls. Any language can use the [HTTP API](/wyrd/api/openapi/), and agents can use the [MCP tools](/wyrd/reference/mcp-tools/) or the `wyrd` CLI.

## Can I run it locally or on my own infrastructure?

Yes. [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/) runs a local server against your PostgreSQL 16 on macOS (Apple silicon) or Linux. [Deploy for a team](/wyrd/operate/deploy-wyrd-for-a-team/) runs it on your own infrastructure with PostgreSQL and an object store.

## Next

Start with the [Quickstart](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/), or read [Foundations of verification](/wyrd/understand/foundations-of-verification/) and [Real-time verification](/wyrd/understand/real-time-verification/) for the ideas behind it.

# Verifier Card

Page: /wyrd/reference/verifier-card/

> Fields, input slots, steps, checks, operators, references, citations, and refusals of a Verifier spec.

A Verifier spec declares the evidence a caller sends, the steps that prepare it, and the requirements that judge it. Every object refuses keys it does not define.

```yaml
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata: {name: follows-policy, version: 1.0.0, space: support}
spec:
  description: A refund decision letter follows the refund policy.
  inputs: {letter: {type: media, formats: [markdown]}}
  steps: [{id: read-letter, action: {kind: extract, from: inputs.letter}}]
  requirements: [{id: follows-policy, statement: "...", check: {kind: agent, agent: ./policy-judge.yaml}}]
  decide: all
```

## Spec fields

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | string | none | One sentence shown with results |
| `inputs` | map of slot name to [input slot](#input-slots) | `{}` | The named evidence a caller sends |
| `steps` | list of [steps](#steps) | `[]` | Work that prepares evidence before requirements run |
| `requirements` | list of [requirements](#requirements) | `[]` | What must be true; each has one check |
| `decide` | [`all` or `{pass_rate: {threshold}}`](#decide) | `all` | How requirement outcomes become the verdict |
| `context_capture` | `full`, `hash`, or `redact` | `full` | How a check's `actual` value is stored: as extracted, as its SHA-256 hex digest, or omitted |

Step and requirement `id`s share one namespace.

## Input slots

A caller fills a slot by name; steps and checks read it as `inputs.<slot>`. A slot the caller omits is missing evidence, never `null`: every check that needs it, including an `is_null` assertion or a step `when` that reads it, is `inconclusive`, while checks that do not need it still run. Slots have no `required` field. To accept `null`, supply it and let the slot's `schema` admit it.

| `type` | Extra fields | Accepts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `json` | `schema` (JSON Schema, optional) | Any JSON value, checked against `schema` when set |
| `media` | `formats` (required), `max_bytes` | A file in one of `formats`, no larger than `max_bytes` |
| `trace` | none | The run's trace spans |
| `samples` | `features` (required) | Feature values over a window, for drift checks |

A `json` or `media` slot may set `deferred: true`: its value is not passed when the execution starts but published later for a pull request's head commit, as in [Publish CI results to a pull request](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/publish-deferred-evidence/). Checks and steps that read a deferred slot wait for it while the rest run; the execution reports `waiting` with the slot names, resumes when the evidence is published, and ends `timed_out` if it never is. A Verifier with a deferred slot is queued only: `verify` refuses it.

A group Verifier slot is a source string instead of an object: `verifiers.<name>.inputs.<slot>` or `verifiers.<name>.requirements.<rid>.outcome`. It holds one value per source execution, in order.

Media formats: `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `webp`, `pdf`, `text`, `markdown`, `csv`, `json`, `html`, `docx`, `xlsx`, `pptx`, `doc`, `xls`, `ppt`, `tar_gz`, `zip`.

## Steps

A step's result is `steps.<id>.output`.

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | required | Name used in references |
| `action` | [action](#actions) | required | What the step does |
| `depends_on` | list of step ids | `[]` | Steps that must finish first |
| `when` | `{path, operator, expected}` | none | Run only if this holds; otherwise the step is skipped and its requirements are `not_applicable` |
| `requirements` | list of [requirements](#requirements) | `[]` | Checked against this step's output, right after it |
| `timeout_seconds` | integer above 0 | none | Time limit for one attempt |
| `retries` | 0 to 5 | `0` | Attempts after the first |

### Actions

When to use each kind is in [Steps and checks](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/#steps-and-checks).

| `kind` | Fields | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `extract` | `from`: a `media` slot | The file's text and structure, in the shape [Extraction output](/wyrd/reference/extraction-output/) gives for its format |
| `extract` | `extractor: pull_request` | The pinned source of the pull request the execution was queued for, described below |
| `agent` | `agent`, `inputs`, `workspace` | The Agent's response, shaped by its Prompt `response_format` |
| `code` | `runtime` (`python`, default), `entrypoint`, `source`, `inputs` | The function's return value, as JSON |
| `approval` | `message` | The decision receipt: `{approval_id, status, actor_id, decided_at, reason}`, `status` `approved` or `rejected` |

- `extract` reads `pdf`, `text`, `markdown`, `csv`, `json`, `html`, `docx`, `xlsx`, and `pptx`, choosing the extractor by format.
- `agent` is a path such as `./reader.yaml` or a CardRef. `inputs` maps each Prompt placeholder to a reference; a placeholder takes text, so a `media` slot goes through `extract` first. `workspace` maps paths under `/inputs/` to a reference such as `inputs.policy`, or to `{artifact: {card: {kind: Artifact, name, version}, path}}`, which mounts one file, a directory, or (without `path`) every file of an uploaded Artifact version, unchanged and pinned with the Verifier. Tools are in [Agent tools and authorization](/wyrd/reference/agent-tools-and-authorization/).
- `extract` with `extractor: pull_request` takes no `from`. It runs only in an execution queued by a [Repository's](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/declare-a-repository/) `pull_request` Trigger, so a Verifier holding it is queued-only: verifying it directly is refused with `WYRD_VERIFICATION_422_INPUT_UNSUPPORTED` before any step runs. Its output is JSON with `format`, `pr` (number, title, body, `base`, `head`, `merge_base`), `review` (`mode`, `comparison_base`, `previous` execution, `fallback_reason`, and the whole pull request as `full_pr`), `changes` (the reviewed range), and `context` (related code with its `omissions`). `changes` and `review.full_pr` are each `{base, head, files}`; every entry in `files` is `{path, previous_path, status, before, after, hunks}`, with `status` one of `added`, `modified`, `deleted`, `renamed` or `type_changed`. `before` is `null` for an added file and `after` is `null` for a deleted one; otherwise a side is `{kind: text, blob, text}`, `{kind: binary, blob}`, `{kind: unavailable, blob, limit_bytes}` or `{kind: excluded, blob, reason}`. The first review, or one after a policy change or when the previous head was rewritten or is unavailable, is `full`, naming why in `fallback_reason` (`first_review`, `policy_changed`, `history_rewritten`, `history_unavailable`); later ones review only the commits since the last execution that extracted source. Pass it to an Agent through `inputs` or `workspace`, for example `workspace: {/inputs/pr.json: steps.pr.output}`. Wyrd never checks out the repository. A binary file, a file over 1 MiB, a symlink, a submodule and vendored or generated files are carried by blob id with `kind` `binary`, `unavailable` or `excluded` instead of text; a changed file GitHub cannot serve fails the step, and an empty change is never a pass. `changes.files` is empty when nothing changed since the previous review, so assert on it rather than on `changes`: `check: {kind: assert, path: steps.pr.output.changes.files, operator: is_non_empty}`. Read the output with `GET /v1/verification/executions/{id}/details`, or the MCP tool `verification.get_execution_details`.
- `approval` waits for a person, as in [Approve a pull request](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/approve-a-pull-request/). Each step, fanout item and repeat iteration it reaches is one occurrence with its own `approval_id`, listed in the execution's `approvals` with `step_id`, `item`, `iteration`, `message` and `status` (`pending`, `approved`, `rejected` or `expired`). Steps that do not depend on it keep running; the execution reports `waiting` while an occurrence is pending and continues under the same ID once it is decided. It has no deadline of its own: when the execution ends or times out, an undecided occurrence is `expired` with no actor. Deciding needs `verifier:approve` on the Verifier and read access to its subject. Completing the step proves nothing; require approval explicitly with `check: {kind: assert, path: steps.<id>.output.status, operator: equals, expected: approved}`, which a rejection fails. A Verifier with an approval step is queued-only: `verify` refuses it.
- `code` calls the function `entrypoint` with `inputs` as keyword arguments. `source` is `{inline: "<python>"}` or `{artifact: {card, path?}}`, where `card` names an Artifact Card.

## Requirements

A requirement ends `passed`, `failed`, `inconclusive`, or `not_applicable`.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | Name in results and in `steps.<id>.requirements.<rid>` |
| `statement` | string | The claim, as a reader sees it in results |
| `check` | [check](#checks) | How the claim is decided |

### Checks

When to use each kind is in [Steps and checks](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/#steps-and-checks).

| `kind` | Fields | Decides by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `assert` | `path` or `each`, `operator`, `expected` | Comparing a value; `each` with `[*]` requires every item to pass |
| `trace` | `on`, `span_selector`, `operator`, `expected` | Comparing values selected from trace spans |
| `agent` | `agent`, `inputs`, `workspace` | An Agent, with its declared tools and optional workspace as in a step, whose Prompt `response_format` is `verdict` or a closed [verdict](#verdicts-and-citations) schema |
| `code` | `runtime`, `source`, `entrypoint`, `inputs`, optional `response_format` | A Python function that returns a verdict |
| `drift` | `on`, `method`, `signal`, `condition`, `profile` | Comparing a window of samples with a baseline |

A `trace` check reads every retained span with the trace ID from `bifrost.traces.spans`, as the executing account, ordered by start time then span ID, up to 10,000 spans. A larger trace, a refused or failed query, a timed-out read, an undecodable span, or an input with no trace makes it `inconclusive`. A trace with no visible span is `inconclusive` under `verify`; in a queued execution, each attempt before the last ends with error code `evidence_unavailable` and status `retrying` (3 attempts, 30 s then 60 s apart), and the last is `inconclusive`. [Trace evidence](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/#trace-evidence) explains the behavior.

A `drift` check judges a scheduled window of `samples`. A Verifier with a `samples` slot or a `drift` check has only those, and is bound with a `schedule` Trigger and no `inputs`. `condition` is `Statistical`. A feature drifts when its score exceeds the threshold, and the requirement fails if any feature drifted; a window with no samples in a slot is `inconclusive`.

| `method` | Scores | `profile` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Psi` | How far each feature's distribution moved from a baseline Data Card named by `signal.baseline_ref` | `binning_strategy` (`EqualWidth` or `Quantile`, 2 to 1000 bins) and `threshold`: `Fixed { value }`, or `ChiSquare { alpha }` / `Normal { alpha }` |
| `Spc` | Control-chart signals on numeric features against a baseline | `{ sample_size }`, at least 2 |
| `Custom` | One metric's mean against a fixed limit, with `signal: { kind: Metric, name }` | `{ metric_name, baseline_value, alert_threshold }`, `metric_name` equal to the signal's name. No baseline |

The server fits a `Psi` or `Spc` baseline after declaration. Its state is the Verifier's `status.verification.baseline.state`: `pending`, `building`, `ready`, or `failed` with `baseline.error`. A window judged before `ready` is `inconclusive`.

## Comparison operators

`assert`, `trace`, and `when` take an operator: its name, such as `operator: not_contains`, or `{kind: <name>, ...}` when it takes parameters.

| Group | Operators |
| --- | --- |
| Comparison | `equals`, `not_equals`, `greater_than`, `greater_than_or_equals`, `less_than`, `less_than_or_equals`, `is_positive`, `is_negative`, `is_zero` |
| String | `contains`, `not_contains`, `contains_ignore_case`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `is_email`, `is_url`, `is_uuid`, `is_ipv4`, `is_ipv6`, `is_json` |
| Collection | `in`, `not_in`, `is_subset`, `is_superset`, `is_disjoint`, `all_of`, `any_of`, `none_of`, `is_empty`, `is_non_empty`, `unique_values` |
| Type | `is_truthy`, `is_falsy`, `is_null`, `is_not_null`, `is_string`, `is_number`, `is_boolean`, `is_object` |

Operators with parameters:

| `kind` | Parameters |
| --- | --- |
| `in_range`, `not_in_range` | `min`, `max`, `inclusive` |
| `approximately_equals`, `within_abs_tolerance` | `tolerance` |
| `within_pct_tolerance` | `pct` |
| `within_std_dev` | `sigma`, `mean`, `std_dev` |
| `between_percentiles` | `lower_pct`, `upper_pct` |
| `divergence_less_than` | `metric` (`kl`, `js`, `wasserstein`), `threshold` |
| `cosine_similarity_at_least` | `threshold` |
| `matches_regex`, `not_matches_regex` | `pattern` |
| `has_min_length` | `min` |
| `has_max_length` | `max` |
| `length` | `expected` |
| `length_greater_than` | `min` |
| `length_less_than` | `max` |
| `is_type` | `expected` (`null`, `bool`, `number`, `string`, `array`, `object`) |

```yaml
check: {kind: assert, path: inputs.refund.amount, operator: {kind: in_range, min: 0, max: 100, inclusive: true}}
```

## References

Every `path`, `each`, `from`, `on`, and `inputs` value is a reference.

| Reference | Reads |
| --- | --- |
| `inputs.<slot>` | An input slot's value |
| `steps.<id>.output` | A step's output |
| `steps.<id>.status` | A step's final status |
| `steps.<id>.requirements.<rid>.outcome` | The outcome of a step's requirement |
| `steps.<id>.requirements.<rid>.reason` | The reason of a step's requirement |
| `requirement.id`, `requirement.statement` | The requirement being checked |

Inputs and step outputs take child selectors: `.field`, `[0]`, and `[*]`. `[*]` is allowed only in an `assert` check's `each`.

## Verdicts and citations

An `agent` or `code` check returns a verdict:

```json
{
  "outcome": "passed",
  "reason": "The 40 dollar refund is approved within 30 days.",
  "citations": [{"slot": "letter", "locator": {"lines": {"start": 3, "end": 4}}}]
}
```

`outcome` is `passed`, `failed`, or `inconclusive`. Each citation names an input `slot` and one `locator`:

| Locator | For |
| --- | --- |
| `{page: n}` | PDF pages, counted from 1 |
| `{slide: n}` | PPTX slides |
| `{lines: {start, end}}` | Text, Markdown, HTML, CSV |
| `{json_pointer: "/path"}` | JSON inputs and DOCX or XLSX extraction output |
| `{region: {page, x, y, width, height}}` | A rectangle on a page, in page coordinates |

A citation names the original slot, or the `attachment_<n>` slot a fixed workspace file reports in `sources`, never an extract step or `/work` file. With `response_format: verdict`, an Agent check's model may cite only the bare slots its inputs and workspace reach, such as `answer`, never `inputs.answer`. An invalid citation is dropped, and a `passed` verdict left without one is recorded as `inconclusive`. For JSON pointers into extracted files, see [Extraction output](/wyrd/reference/extraction-output/#citations).

### Custom data

`response_format: verdict` (or `{kind: verdict}`) asks for exactly the verdict above. `{kind: verdict, data: <JSON Schema>}` also requires a `data` object matching that object schema, written in JSON Schema 2020-12 (omit `$schema` or declare 2020-12) and without a root `$id`. An Agent declares it on its Prompt; a `code` check declares it on the check, beside `entrypoint`, and returns `data` in its verdict. Without a `data` schema, a verdict must not carry `data`.

An Agent step's Prompt may instead declare `response_format: code_review`, the standard code review report Wyrd renders on a pull request's Check and review; it takes no `data`. See [Review a pull request](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/review-a-pull-request/).

The server validates the whole verdict against the declared schema. Data must fit both limits, inclusive:

| Limit | Bound |
| --- | --- |
| Size | 65,536 bytes of compact UTF-8 JSON |
| Depth | 16 containers; the root object is one, each nested object or array adds one |

An Agent answer that fails its schema is returned to the model with a correction, and each correction spends one of the Agent's `max_iterations`. An answer still invalid on the last iteration, or a provider refusal, which is never corrected, makes the requirement `inconclusive` with `WYRD_AGENT_422_STRUCTURED_INVALID` in its reason. A `code` check's verdict is never corrected. A verdict that fails its schema or a limit makes the requirement `inconclusive` with no `data`; the reason names the location or limit, never the content. Accepted data is the requirement result's `data`, on step and Verifier requirements alike, and is kept with the rest of the result.

## Decide

| Value | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| `all` | `failed` if any requirement fails; otherwise `inconclusive` if any is inconclusive; otherwise `passed` |
| `{pass_rate: {threshold}}` | `passed` when the passed share of applicable requirements, inconclusive ones included in the count, reaches `threshold`; `threshold` is above 0 and at most 1 |

`not_applicable` requirements are excluded. With no applicable requirement, the verdict is `inconclusive`.

## Rejections

| Code | Raised when |
| --- | --- |
| `WYRD_LOADER_400_INVALID_ENVELOPE` | `wyrd declare` refused the Card tree; each problem is one entry in `details.diagnostics` with its own code |
| `WYRD_REGISTRY_400_INVALID_CARD_SPEC` | The server refused a registered spec whose field is unknown, missing, or has the wrong type |
| `WYRD_SPEC_400_VALIDATION` | A rule fails; its `rule` and `path` are in `details`, or in a `wyrd declare` diagnostic's `context` |

Common `rule` values in `WYRD_SPEC_400_VALIDATION`:

| `rule` | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `unknown_reference` | A reference names an input, step, or requirement that does not exist |
| `duplicate_id` | Two steps or requirements share an `id` |
| `graph` | `depends_on` forms a cycle |
| `media_as_text` | A `media` slot is bound to an Agent text placeholder |
| `extract_source` | An `extract` step names both or neither of `from` and `extractor`, or `from` is not a whole `media` slot |
| `extract_format` | An `extract` step reads a slot with a format it cannot extract |
| `operator` | An operator's parameters are invalid, such as a bad regex |
| `step_budget` | `timeout_seconds` is 0 or `retries` is above 5 |
| `pass_rate` | `threshold` is not above 0 and at most 1 |
| `check_response_format` | A `code` check's `response_format` names an unknown format or an invalid `data` schema |
| `check_agent_schema` | A check Agent's Prompt cannot produce a verdict, or declares `data` without requiring an object |

# Extraction output

Page: /wyrd/reference/extraction-output/

> The JSON an extract step returns for each media format.

An `extract` step returns JSON whose shape depends on the file's format. Every field is always present: an empty list is `[]`, empty text is `""`, and `null` appears only where the type allows it. Types are TypeScript notation for the wire JSON.

## PDF

```typescript
type PdfOutput = { format: "pdf"; pages: { number: number; text: string }[] };
```

`number` starts at 1. `text` is `""` for a page with no text layer, such as a scan.

## PPTX

```typescript
type PptxOutput = {
  format: "pptx";
  slides: {
    number: number;
    title: string | null;
    paragraphs: string[];
    tables: { rows: string[][] }[];
    notes: string;
  }[];
};
```

- Slides are in presentation order; `number` starts at 1.
- `title` is the title placeholder's text, lines joined by `\n`, or `null`.
- `paragraphs` holds the other non-empty paragraphs, not table text. `notes` is `""` when there are none.

## DOCX

```typescript
type DocxOutput = {
  format: "docx";
  blocks: ({ kind: "paragraph"; text: string; style: string | null } | { kind: "table"; rows: string[][] })[];
};
```

- Blocks are the document body in order, including content controls. Headers, footers, footnotes, and comments are not read.
- `style` is Word's style ID, such as `Heading1`, or `null`.

## XLSX

```typescript
type XlsxOutput = {
  format: "xlsx";
  sheets: {
    name: string;
    cells: { address: string; value: string | number | boolean | null; formula: string | null; error: string | null }[];
  }[];
};
```

- Sheets are in workbook order; cells row by row, left to right. Empty cells are left out, so look a cell up by `address`, such as `B2`.
- `value` is the stored value, or a formula's last saved result; formulas are never recalculated. Dates are Excel serial numbers.
- `formula` is the formula text with a leading `=`, or `null`.
- An error cell has `value: null` and the error, such as `#DIV/0!`, in `error`.

## CSV

```typescript
type CsvOutput = { format: "csv"; rows: string[][] };
```

Every row, including the header. Every cell is a string.

## JSON

```typescript
type JsonOutput = { format: "json"; value: JsonValue };
```

## Text, Markdown, HTML

```typescript
type TextOutput = { format: "text" | "markdown" | "html"; text: string };
```

The file unchanged; Markdown and HTML are not parsed.

## Tables

In PPTX and DOCX tables, a merged cell's text is in its top-left position and the positions it covers are `""`, so every row has the same length.

## Paths

Read fields as `steps.<id>.output.pages[0].text`. Indexes are zero-based. `[*]` is allowed only in an `assert` check's `each`.

## Citations

A `json_pointer` locator addresses this extracted JSON for DOCX and XLSX, such as `/blocks/0/text`, and the parsed document for JSON. Other locators are in [Verifier Card](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/#verdicts-and-citations).

## Not extracted

| Input | Instead |
| --- | --- |
| `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `webp` | No OCR or rendering; give the file to an Agent as `media` |
| `doc`, `xls`, `ppt` | Convert to `docx`, `xlsx`, or `pptx` |
| `zip`, `tar_gz` | Put them in an Agent's `workspace` |

## Failures

The step fails, and the requirements that need it are `inconclusive`, when:

| Condition | Formats |
| --- | --- |
| The file does not parse as its format | All |
| The PDF is encrypted | `pdf` |
| The text is not UTF-8 | `text`, `markdown`, `html` |
| The archive exceeds `WYRD_VERIFICATION_ARCHIVE_MAX_ENTRIES`, `WYRD_VERIFICATION_ARCHIVE_MAX_MIB`, or `WYRD_VERIFICATION_ARCHIVE_MAX_RATIO` | `docx`, `xlsx`, `pptx` |
| Pages or slides exceed `WYRD_VERIFICATION_EXTRACT_MAX_PAGES` | `pdf`, `pptx` |
| Extracted text exceeds `WYRD_VERIFICATION_EXTRACT_TEXT_MAX_MIB` | All |

Limits are in [Verification runtime limits](/wyrd/reference/verification-runtime-limits/). Each result records the extractor version `wyrd-extract/1`.

# Agent tools

Page: /wyrd/reference/agent-tools-and-authorization/

> Built-in tools a Verifier's Agent can call and the permissions each call needs.

A Verifier's Agent calls server built-in tools, named in its `tool_names`. There is no fetch tool and no network access.

## Built-in tools

| Tool | Does | Resource permission |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cards.list` | Lists Card summaries by kind, name, space, or metadata | `cards:read` |
| `cards.get` | Reads one Card by exact kind, name, version, and space, or by kind and UID | `cards:read` |
| `bifrost.list_tables` | Lists tables | `bifrost_table:read` |
| `bifrost.describe_table` | Reads one table's schema | `bifrost_table:read` |
| `bifrost.query` | Runs one read-only SQL query | `bifrost_query:read` on every table it reads |
| `fs.list` | Lists workspace files | Workspace only |
| `fs.read` | Reads a UTF-8 workspace file's actual lines, with `lines` locators and a resumable `next` | Workspace only |
| `fs.search` | Finds matching lines: literal and case-insensitive by default, or `regex`, `case_sensitive`, a `path` file or directory scope, and a filename `glob` | Workspace only |
| `fs.extract` | Extracts one supported `/inputs` document to a new `/work` `output_path` as extraction JSON | Workspace only |
| `fs.write` | Creates or replaces one UTF-8 file under `/work`, creating its parent directories, and returns `path` and `bytes` | Workspace only |
| `code.run` | Runs sandboxed Python against the workspace, which can call the Agent's other declared tools except `fs.write` and `publish` | Workspace only; each call from Python needs that tool's grants |
| `publish` | Retains one `/work` file or directory, or one JSON value, under a logical `name` for the steps that read this step's publications; returns `{name, kind}` | Step Agents only |

Arguments are capped by `WYRD_VERIFICATION_TOOL_ARGUMENT_MAX_KIB`, results by `WYRD_VERIFICATION_TOOL_RESULT_MAX_KIB`, and one Agent step or check, across its retries, makes at most `WYRD_VERIFICATION_AGENT_TOOL_MAX_CALLS` calls, direct and from Python together ([limits](/wyrd/reference/verification-runtime-limits/)).

Each call is recorded in `tool_calls` in the execution's details (`Execution.details`, or `verification.get_execution_details` over MCP): on the step for a step Agent, on the requirement for a check Agent. A record has `tool`, `arguments`, `recipient`, `output_sha256` (absent when nothing was returned), `returned_bytes`, and `error` (present when the call failed). `recipient` is `model` for a call the model made and `code` for a call a `code.run` program made; a record written before `recipient` existed reads as `model`. A requirement written before check records existed has no `tool_calls`.

## Tools from Python

A `code.run` program calls a declared tool with `await call_tool(name, arguments)` and gets the tool's result as Python values. It can call any tool in the Agent's `tool_names` except `code.run`, `fs.write`, and `publish`, which only the model calls. Each call runs exactly as if the model had made it, with the same grants, limits, and audit, and is recorded with recipient `code`.

The model sees the `code.run` result: `output`, what the program printed, and `value`, the repr of its last expression, each cut at `WYRD_VERIFICATION_TOOL_RESULT_MAX_KIB`, with `value_truncated` set when `value` was cut. Any other intermediate result stays in Python, so a program can read many files or rows and return a short answer in one model turn. A program that prints a tool result, or ends with an expression holding one, sends it to the model. Citations still point to the original pinned evidence, such as an `/inputs` file and its lines, never to the program's output.

```python title="code.run source"
# What a model sends as code.run source: read a Card, then query Bifrost.
# A denied call raises RuntimeError carrying the catalog problem JSON, so the
# program can branch on its code and carry on without the protected value.
import json

card = await call_tool('cards.get', {'card_ref': {'kind': 'Service', 'name': 'policy-desk', 'version': '1.0.0'}})
try:
    await call_tool('bifrost.query', {'sql': 'SELECT execution_id FROM bifrost.verification.results LIMIT 1', 'max_rows': 1})
    query = 'allowed'
    again = None
except RuntimeError as error:
    query = json.loads(str(error))['code']
    again = await call_tool('cards.get', {'card_ref': {'kind': 'Service', 'name': 'policy-desk', 'version': '1.0.0'}})
# The model sees what the program prints and the repr of its last expression,
# here None; every other value stays in Python.
print('query', query, 'repaired', again == card)

```

A failed call raises `RuntimeError`. Its message is the call's problem JSON, with `code`, `status`, `title`, `detail`, `remediation`, and `details`; branch on `code` and carry on, as above. A denied call returns no data, so the program cannot read the protected value. Two failures end the step or check instead and cannot be caught: spending the call limit, and a server stop such as a capacity refusal.

Fewer model turns are not guaranteed to cost fewer tokens or less time: the program's source and its `code.run` result still pass through the model, and the Python worker stays busy while the program waits on tools.

## Rules

- `fs.write`, `code.run`, and `publish` get private `/work` scratch without a `workspace`. `fs.list`, `fs.read`, `fs.search`, and `fs.extract` need a `workspace` or one of `fs.write` and `code.run` beside them. A `workspace` needs a tool that uses it.
- `/work` belongs to one invocation attempt. A later step, a retry, or a sibling never sees it; only what `publish` accepts reaches other steps.
- Each tool is named once. The provider-facing spelling, such as `fs_write`, is not a tool name.
- Step and check Agents follow the same rules, except that only a step Agent may declare `publish`. Each call still needs its grants.
- Nothing is parsed unless the Agent calls `fs.extract`; `fs.read` and `fs.search` serve raw text and refuse or skip binary files.

## Permissions

Every call needs both a `tool:invoke` grant and the tool's resource permission. Neither implies the other.

```json
{"resource":"tool","action":"invoke","scope":"all"}
{"resource":"tool","action":"invoke","scope":{"tool":"bifrost.query"}}
```

The scope is `all` or one exact tool name, never a pattern. A call runs as the principal that started the verification, or the binding owner for a scheduled one; delegation can narrow that authority but never widen it. `verifier:run` and declaring a tool grant nothing.

## Publishing

`publish` takes a `name` matching `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$` and exactly one source: `path`, an existing `/work` file or whole directory, or `value`, any JSON value including `null`. A path is snapshotted when the call runs, so later writes do not change the publication; directories keep empty subdirectories and their actual filenames. The receipt is `{"name": ..., "kind": "file" | "directory" | "json"}` and is returned only after the execution accepts the publication.

A name is unique within one step attempt: publishing it again in that attempt is refused, while a fresh retry of the step may reuse it and is attributed to its own attempt. The server records the producing step, item, iteration, and attempt; no argument can set them. A replayed provider tool call returns its original receipt. A final answer is not a publication.

A later step mounts `steps.<id>.publications.<name>` or the whole `steps.<id>.publications` collection, whose `manifest.json` lists each entry's actual path. A step whose named publication is missing fails before its model call. Publications read back through the execution's publication endpoints with their manifests and download plans.

Publications belong to queued executions. Registration marks a Verifier `queue_only` when one of its step or check Agents, inline or a referenced registered Agent, declares `publish`; the server sets this flag and ignores any value you send. A `verify` call for such a Verifier is refused with `WYRD_VERIFICATION_422_INPUT_UNSUPPORTED` before any step runs; submit it instead. A `verify` execution has no invocation or publication history, so those endpoints answer it as not found.

## Failed tool calls

A failed call does not end the step. The model, or the program for a call from Python, receives `code`, `error`, and, for a call it can repair, `details`, then may call again; the call's `tool_calls` record keeps the `error`. An `fs.*` or `publish` call that breaks one of the rules below returns `WYRD_SPEC_400_VALIDATION` with `details` naming the `rule`, the argument `field`, its `value`, and what was `expected`. A local IO failure returns `SKALD_TOOL_500_CALL` without `details`.

| Rule | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `workspace_path` | A path is not under `/inputs` or `/work`, or has an empty, `.`, or `..` segment |
| `workspace_missing` | No file or directory exists at the path |
| `regular_file` | A file argument names a directory or a non-regular file |
| `utf8_text` | `fs.read` names a file that is not UTF-8 text |
| `result_limit` | The `fs.read` path is too long for any line to fit within the tool result limit |
| `search_query` | `fs.search` has an empty `query` |
| `search_pattern` | A `regex` query is not valid Rust regex syntax |
| `search_glob` | `glob` is not a relative glob without `..` segments |
| `extractable_document` | `fs.extract` names a file that is not an extractable document |
| `extraction_refused` | `fs.extract` names a malformed document or one over the extraction limits |
| `output_path` | `output_path` is not a new file path under `/work` |
| `output_exists` | `output_path` already exists |
| `work_budget` | The file, the written content, or the extraction exceeds the `/work` write budget |
| `write_path` | `fs.write` names `/inputs`, `/work` itself, or a path outside `/work` or with an empty, `.`, or `..` segment |
| `write_parent` | An `fs.write` parent is a file or a link |
| `publication_path` | `publish` names a `path` outside `/work` |
| `publication_source` | `publish` has both or neither of `path` and `value` |
| `publication_name` | The `name` was already published in this step attempt |
| `publication_tree` | A published directory holds an entry the tree rules refuse |
| `publication_size` | A published `value` or file exceeds its limit |
| `publication_count`, `publication_bytes` | The execution's publications would exceed their count or retained-byte limit |

## Errors

| Code | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `WYRD_PERMISSION_403_DENIED_RBAC` | The principal lacks `tool:invoke` or the resource permission; the call returns no data |
| `WYRD_AGENT_404_TOOL_NOT_IN_AGENT` | A program called a tool not in the Agent's `tool_names`, or `code.run`, `fs.write`, or `publish` |
| `WYRD_TOOL_422_INPUT` | A program passed arguments that are not a JSON object, or a call's arguments exceed `WYRD_VERIFICATION_TOOL_ARGUMENT_MAX_KIB` |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_422_TOOL_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` | The step or check spent `WYRD_VERIFICATION_AGENT_TOOL_MAX_CALLS`; the step fails or the check is `inconclusive`, with no further model turn |
| `WYRD_SPEC_400_VALIDATION`, rule `agent_tools` | Unknown or repeated tool name, a reading `fs.*` tool without a workspace or scratch writer, a workspace without a tool that uses it, or `publish` on a check Agent |
| `WYRD_SPEC_400_VALIDATION`, rule `workspace_path` | A `workspace` key is not `/inputs/<name>[/<name>...]`, contains `.` or `..`, or overlaps another mount |
| `WYRD_SPEC_400_VALIDATION`, rule `workspace_artifact` | A workspace `artifact` selection does not reference an Artifact Card |

# Runtime limits

Page: /wyrd/reference/verification-runtime-limits/

> Server settings that bound Verifier files, extraction, workspaces, Python code, model calls, and direct and queued executions, with defaults and startup rules.

Environment variables on `wyrd-server`, read once at startup; a change takes a restart. Execution slots, model calls, and the queued execution timeout can also be set in the [server TOML file](#server-toml-file); the other settings are environment variables only. Each process applies them on its own.

## Settings

| Variable | Default | Bounds |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_ENABLED` | `1` | Whether an API-serving process runs Verifiers: `1` or `0`. Also `[verification] enabled` in TOML |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_TIMEOUT_MS` | 60000 | The whole `verify` call |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_MS` | 300000 | One queued execution, from its first claim; waiting and retries do not reset it |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_DIRECT_EXECUTIONS` | 256 | `verify` calls running at once in one server process |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_QUEUED_EXECUTIONS` | 64 | Queued executions running at once in one server process; more wait in the queue |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_FILE_MAX_MIB` | 20 | One input file, and one file a publication retains |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_FILES_MAX_MIB` | 100 | All input files of one request or one workspace together, and all bytes one execution's publications retain |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_PUBLICATIONS_MAX` | 1000 | Publications one execution accepts across all its attempts |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_ARCHIVE_MAX_MIB` | 200 | Decompressed bytes of one archive, including DOCX, XLSX, and PPTX containers |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_ARCHIVE_MAX_ENTRIES` | 10000 | Entries in one archive |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_ARCHIVE_MAX_RATIO` | 100 | Decompressed-to-compressed size ratio of one archive |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_EXTRACT_MAX_PAGES` | 500 | PDF pages or PPTX slides in one extraction |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_EXTRACT_TEXT_MAX_MIB` | 10 | Text produced by one extraction |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_SCRATCH_MAX_MIB` | 250 | All bytes in one workspace: materialized `/inputs` plus `/work` |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_WORK_WRITE_MAX_MIB` | 50 | Bytes held under `/work` in one workspace |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_TOOL_RESULT_MAX_KIB` | 64 | One tool result or one Python operation's printed output, cut off while it is collected |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_MODEL_CALLS` | 256 | Gateway model calls `verify` calls and queued executions make at once in one server process; another waits for one to finish |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_TOOL_ARGUMENT_MAX_KIB` | 64 | One tool call's arguments as compact JSON, `code.run` source included |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_AGENT_TOOL_MAX_CALLS` | 128 | Tool calls of one Agent step or check, from the model and from Python together, across its retries |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_MONTY_MIN_WORKERS` | 1 | Python workers prewarmed with the server, as many as fit in process memory; stopped when an operation needs their memory |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_MONTY_MEMORY_MIB` | 256 | Memory one Python operation may allocate |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_CODE_TIMEOUT_MS` | 10000 | One Python operation, from waiting for a worker through compiling, running, its file calls, and its waits on `call_tool` |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_AGENT_CODE_BUDGET_MS` | 60000 | All `code.run` calls of one Agent step together, waits on `call_tool` included, across its retries |

`_MIB` and `_KIB` are binary units; `_MS` is milliseconds. A `media` slot's `max_bytes` can lower `FILE_MAX_MIB` for that slot, never raise it. No setting disables a limit or worker isolation.

## Direct and queued capacity

`verify` calls and queued executions share one process's Python pool, CPU turns, model calls, memory, and scratch, charged only while in use; nothing is reserved for either. `DIRECT_EXECUTIONS` and `QUEUED_EXECUTIONS` cap how many of each run at once and hold nothing while idle. A queued execution resumed after it waited, was deferred, or was retried is admitted again. Both run the same engine with the same authority, evidence, billing, and cancellation rules, and every model call still passes the gateway's own tenant and subject limits and budgets.

A deployment may also run `direct` and `worker` processes separately (see [deployment targets](/wyrd/understand/architecture/#one-binary-several-roles)). Postgres, the gateway, and model providers stay shared.

The defaults give each process headroom to start from, not measured throughput or latency guarantees, and not every mix of workloads is guaranteed to fit a host.

`EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_MS` is the ceiling of one queued execution from its first claim. Waiting for capacity, deferrals, and retries count against it and never reset it; anything an execution waits for, including an intended human approval period, must fit inside it.

## Server TOML file

`wyrd-server` reads the first file found, in this order. Environment variables override its values.

| Order | File |
| ---: | --- |
| 1 | The path in `WYRD_CONFIG_PATH`; startup fails if it does not exist |
| 2 | `/etc/wyrd/server.toml` |
| 3 | `~/.config/wyrd/server.toml` |

With no file, the server uses its defaults and environment variables.

Under `[verification]`, the file can set the execution slots, model calls, and the queued execution timeout. The matching environment variable overrides each value on its own, and a value left out keeps its default.

| TOML key | Environment variable |
| --- | --- |
| `[verification] direct_executions` | `WYRD_VERIFICATION_DIRECT_EXECUTIONS` |
| `[verification] queued_executions` | `WYRD_VERIFICATION_QUEUED_EXECUTIONS` |
| `[verification] execution_timeout_ms` | `WYRD_VERIFICATION_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_MS` |
| `[verification] model_calls` | `WYRD_VERIFICATION_MODEL_CALLS` |

```toml
[verification]
direct_executions = 256
queued_executions = 64
execution_timeout_ms = 300000
model_calls = 256
```

## Startup rules

The server refuses to start, naming the variable, when a value is empty, not a positive integer, or overflows once scaled to bytes, or when `WYRD_VERIFICATION_ENABLED` is not `1` or `0`. A TOML value is checked only when no environment variable overrides it, so a valid variable replaces a stale file value; a winning TOML value that is zero or overflows is refused naming its key, and a negative one fails to parse. Whichever source wins is also refused, naming it, when an execution, workspace, or model-call count exceeds 2305843009213693951, the most permits the runtime can hold, or when the queued execution timeout would end after the latest timestamp the queue can represent, about the year 262000. The combinations below are checked after file and environment values are merged, whichever source set them, and are refused naming both variables (prefix `WYRD_VERIFICATION_` omitted):

- `FILE_MAX_MIB` above `FILES_MAX_MIB`
- `WORK_WRITE_MAX_MIB` above `SCRATCH_MAX_MIB`

A process that runs Verifiers also refuses to start when process memory cannot hold one Python session envelope: twice `MONTY_MEMORY_MIB` + 4 MiB of allocator headroom, plus 32 MiB for the worker, which is 552 MiB at the defaults.
